item.title: C Function Argument Evaluation Order Unspecified Undefined Behavior Explained
item.description:
“C Function Argument Evaluation Order Unspecified Undefined Behavior Explained”

In C programming, when you call a function, how are the arguments evaluated? Is there a predictable order? This is a crucial point that often leads to confusion and subtle bugs, particularly when arguments involve side effects like incrementing or decrementing variables. Let’s delve into the specifics of C’s function argument evaluation and the implications of unspecified and undefined behavior.

Is Function Argument Evaluation Order Defined in C?

The short answer is no. The C standard explicitly states that the order of evaluation for function arguments, as well as the order in which subexpressions within those arguments are evaluated, is unspecified. This means different compilers, or even different versions of the same compiler, might evaluate these arguments in varying orders.

This exploration delves into the primary concerns surrounding eval(parse(...)), including security implications, debugging difficulties, and performance considerations, while also presenting more robust alternatives for dynamic code execution in R.

item.title: Why does printf not flush after the call unless a newline is in the format string
item.description:

When working with C programs, particularly when directing output to files or interacting with the system, you might encounter a situation where your printf statements don’t appear on the console immediately as you expect. item.title: C Uninitialized Variables: Static vs. Automatic Scope
item.description:
“C Uninitialized Variables: Static vs. Automatic Scope”

What happens to uninitialized static and global variables in C?

Variables declared with static storage duration, whether at file scope (global) or function scope, are implicitly initialized to zero. This applies to arithmetic types, which become zero, and pointer types, which become a null pointer constant. This initialization is a guarantee provided by the C standard.

Example:

// File scope (global)
int global_counter; // Implicitly initialized to 0

void setup() {
    static int file_scoped_static; // Implicitly initialized to 0
    // ...
}

int main() {
    // ...
    return 0;
}

The C standard, in sections like C89 (6.5.7 Initialization) and C99 (6.7.8 Initialization), explicitly states that static storage duration objects not initialized explicitly are initialized implicitly. For arithmetic types, this means they are assigned zero. This behavior is consistent across different compilers and architectures because the C language standard mandates it.
